title: Oral mucosal conditions & infections
blurb: Thrush, cold sores, mouth ulcers, lichen planus, white and red patches and angular cheilitis: what they look like, what causes them and when they matter.
question: A 78-year-old patient wears her full upper denture day and night. The palate under the denture is red and sore, the corners of her mouth are cracked and red, and she has just finished a course of antibiotics. What is the likely cause, and what advice will support the dentist's treatment?

teach.body: The oral mucosa is the soft lining of the mouth. Changes in it can be infections (fungal or viral), immune conditions, or potentially malignant patches that could turn into cancer. Many are clues to general health: thrush can point to diabetes or a weakened immune system, and recurrent ulcers to anaemia or coeliac disease. The dentist diagnoses. You help by recording findings accurately, following infection control, reinforcing advice and flagging anything the patient mentions.

Candida albicans is a yeast that lives harmlessly in many mouths. It overgrows when defences drop: dentures worn overnight or poorly cleaned, broad-spectrum antibiotics, steroid inhalers, diabetes, dry mouth, a weakened immune system, and the very young or old. Forms include white curds that wipe off leaving a red base, a red sore palate under a denture (denture stomatitis, often painless), and angular cheilitis: cracked red corners of the mouth, often with Staphylococcus aureus too and made worse by worn dentures that let the mouth over-close.

teach.h: Colour clues the dentist looks for

items.label: White, won't wipe off
items.sub: Leukoplakia, lichen planus or hyperplastic candidosis

teach.caption: Whether a white patch wipes off is a key question: thrush usually does; leukoplakia and lichen planus do not.
Any ulcer that has not healed in three weeks needs the dentist's urgent attention, whatever it looked like at first.

teach.body: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is often first caught in childhood, sometimes as primary herpetic gingivostomatitis: fever, swollen gums and many small ulcers. The virus then lies dormant in a nerve and reactivates as cold sores (herpes labialis), triggered by sunlight, colds and fever, stress, tiredness or periods. Blisters contain live virus and are very infectious. The dentist will often postpone routine treatment while a cold sore is active, to avoid spreading it around the patient's mouth and face or to the team.

Oral lichen planus is a long-term immune condition: lacy white lines (Wickham's striae), usually on both cheeks, sometimes with painful red erosive areas. Some patients have itchy purple spots on the skin, often the wrists. Similar 'lichenoid' reactions can follow some medicines or sit next to amalgam fillings. It carries a small cancer risk, so it is reviewed regularly. Recurrent aphthous ulcers are not infectious; triggers include stress, minor injury, iron, B12 or folate deficiency, and coeliac or Crohn's disease.

teach.caption: Both are potentially malignant disorders. Leukoplakia is a white patch that cannot be explained as any other condition.

teach.h: A white patch in a smoker
teach.caption: A white patch on the lower lip of a smoker, with tobacco staining on the teeth. A persistent white patch like this needs the dentist to assess it for leukoplakia.

teach.text: Cold sores are viral and contagious; aphthous ulcers are not infectious at all. Don't mix them up when a patient asks if they can pass on their mouth ulcers.

items: Candida thrives with dentures worn overnight, antibiotics, steroid inhalers, diabetes and dry mouth.
Angular cheilitis: cracked corners; Candida and Staph; worn dentures, anaemia, diabetes.
Cold sores (HSV-1): contagious blisters; triggers include sun, illness and stress.
Aphthous ulcers: not infectious; minor ones heal in 1–2 weeks.
Lichen planus: lacy white lines on both cheeks; reviewed regularly.
Leukoplakia (white) and erythroplakia (red, higher risk) are potentially malignant.

summary: You can now sort common mucosal conditions into infections, immune conditions and potentially malignant patches, recognise the colour clues for each, explain what makes thrush and angular cheilitis likely, tell cold sores from aphthous ulcers, and give practical advice such as removing dentures at night and rinsing after a steroid inhaler.

A.q: A patient wears a full upper denture day and night. The palate directly under the denture is red but not painful. What is the most likely cause?
A.why: Denture stomatitis is a Candida infection under a denture, encouraged by wearing it overnight and poor denture hygiene. It is often painless.

whyNot.0: Lichen planus usually shows as lacy white lines on both cheeks.
whyNot.2: Herpes causes painful blisters and ulcers, not a red area matching the denture.
whyNot.3: Aphthous ulcers are discrete round ulcers, not redness under a denture.

A.q: A patient arrives for a scale and polish with a weeping cold sore on her lip. Why might the dentist postpone routine treatment?
options: The sore is a sign of oral cancer
Local anaesthetic won't work near it
The virus in the blister is contagious
Cold sores are caused by poor oral hygiene
A.why: Active cold sores contain live herpes simplex virus, which can spread to other areas of the patient's face or to the dental team.

whyNot.0: Cold sores are a viral infection, not a sign of cancer.
whyNot.1: This is not the reason; the concern is spreading infection.
whyNot.3: Cold sores are caused by reactivation of HSV-1, not poor oral hygiene.

A.q: The dentist notes lacy white lines on the inside of both cheeks. The patient also has itchy purple spots on her wrists. Which condition is most likely?
A.why: Lacy white striae on both cheeks, sometimes with purple itchy skin lesions, are typical of lichen planus.

whyNot.0: Thrush gives white curds that wipe off, not lacy lines.
whyNot.1: Erythroplakia is a red velvety patch, not white lines.
whyNot.2: Herpes labialis is a cold sore on the lip.

B.q: After a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics, a patient has creamy white patches that wipe off to leave a red, raw surface. What is this most likely to be?
B.why: Antibiotics upset the normal oral flora, letting Candida overgrow. White curds that wipe off are typical of thrush.

whyNot.1: Leukoplakia does not rub or wipe off.
whyNot.2: Lichen planus gives lacy white lines that don't wipe off.
whyNot.3: Frictional keratosis is a white patch from rubbing and does not wipe off.

B.q: A patient with recurrent mouth ulcers asks whether she could pass them on to her children. Which reply is correct for minor aphthous ulcers?
B.why: Aphthous ulcers are an immune condition and are not infectious.

whyNot.0: That is true of cold sores (HSV-1), not aphthous ulcers.
whyNot.1: Aphthous ulcers cannot be passed on by any route.
whyNot.3: They are never infectious, at any stage.

B.q: Which oral patch carries the highest risk of becoming malignant?
options: A white patch from cheek biting
A white curd that wipes away
Lacy white lines on the cheeks
B.why: Erythroplakia is rare but has the highest risk of dysplasia or cancer of all the oral patches.

whyNot.0: Frictional white patches from biting are benign and resolve when the habit stops.
whyNot.1: A white curd that wipes away is thrush, an infection.
whyNot.2: Lichen planus has only a small cancer risk.

C.q: An older patient with a worn, over-closed set of dentures has red, cracked corners of the mouth. What is this condition called?
C.why: Angular cheilitis is inflammation at the corners of the mouth, usually Candida and/or Staphylococcus aureus, encouraged by saliva pooling where worn dentures let the face over-close.

whyNot.0: Herpes labialis (cold sore) is a blistering lesion on the lip, not symmetrical cracked corners.
whyNot.2: A denture granuloma is overgrowth of tissue at a denture flange.
whyNot.3: Geographic tongue is a harmless pattern of smooth red patches on the tongue.

C.q: A patient with asthma uses a steroid inhaler and keeps getting oral thrush. Which advice will help most?
options: Stop the inhaler when thrush appears
Use an alcohol mouthwash each night
Rinse with water after each use
Brush the teeth just before each puff
C.why: Rinsing the mouth with water after a steroid inhaler removes steroid deposits that encourage Candida.

whyNot.0: Patients must never stop asthma medication without medical advice.
whyNot.1: Alcohol mouthwashes can dry the mouth, which favours Candida.
whyNot.3: Brushing before use does not remove the steroid left after the puff.

C.q: Which is a common trigger for a cold sore to come back?
C.why: UV light is a well-known trigger for HSV-1 to reactivate, along with colds, fever, stress and tiredness.

whyNot.1: Dentures are linked to Candida, not herpes reactivation.
whyNot.2: Iron deficiency is linked to aphthous ulcers and angular cheilitis.
whyNot.3: Steroid inhalers are linked to thrush, not cold sores.

reteach.title: Three questions for any mouth lesion
reteach.question: Instead of memorising a list, ask three questions about each condition: is it catching, is it a warning sign, and what is feeding it?

blocks.body: Is it CATCHING? Cold sores are; everything else here mostly is not, so standard precautions cover them. Is it a WARNING? Red and white patches that won't wipe off may be early cancer, and lichen planus needs review. What is FEEDING it? Thrush and angular cheilitis are fed by dentures worn overnight, antibiotics, inhalers, dry mouth or diabetes, so fixing the cause is half the treatment.

blocks.text: A white patch that wipes off is usually thrush. A white patch that does NOT wipe off must be shown to the dentist.

explain.body: Candida overgrows when defences drop. Advise denture wearers to take dentures out at night, clean them and brush the palate. Inhaler users should rinse after use. The dentist may prescribe an antifungal (such as miconazole, nystatin or fluconazole). Miconazole interacts with warfarin, so the medical history matters.

test.q: What denture advice best helps prevent denture stomatitis?
options: Wear the denture overnight to protect the gums
Rinse the denture in hot water once a week
Remove and clean the denture every night
Soak the denture in mouthwash all day
test.why: Leaving dentures out at night and cleaning them daily stops Candida building up on the fitting surface and palate.

whyNot.0: Overnight wear is a major cause of denture stomatitis.
whyNot.1: Weekly rinsing is not enough, and very hot water can warp acrylic.
whyNot.3: Dentures should be cleaned and the tissues rested; soaking all day isn't the answer.

explain.body: HSV-1 lies dormant in a nerve after the first infection. Triggers reactivate it: a tingle, then blisters, then a crust, healing in about 7–10 days. Blisters are highly infectious, so routine treatment is often postponed.

test.q: Which virus causes cold sores on the lip?
test.why: Cold sores (herpes labialis) are usually caused by reactivation of HSV-1.

whyNot.1: HPV causes warts and is linked to oropharyngeal cancer.
whyNot.2: Hepatitis B is a blood-borne virus affecting the liver.
whyNot.3: Varicella zoster causes chickenpox and shingles, not cold sores.

explain.body: Aphthous ulcers are round, yellow-grey with a red halo, usually on the soft inner cheeks and lips, and are not infectious. Minor ones heal in 1–2 weeks. Traumatic ulcers match their cause, such as a sharp tooth or denture edge, and heal once it is fixed.

test.q: A patient gets crops of round, painful ulcers with a red halo several times a year. Which could be an underlying cause the dentist might ask the GP to check?
test.why: Recurrent aphthous ulcers can be linked to deficiencies of iron, vitamin B12 or folate, and to coeliac or Crohn's disease.

whyNot.0: High blood pressure is not a cause of aphthous ulcers.
whyNot.2: Cholesterol levels are not linked to mouth ulcers.
whyNot.3: Hay fever is not a recognised cause of aphthous ulcers.

explain.h: Lichen planus and potentially malignant patches
explain.body: Lichen planus shows lacy white lines on both cheeks and is reviewed regularly. Leukoplakia is a white patch that won't rub off and can't be explained otherwise. Erythroplakia is a red velvety patch and carries the highest cancer risk. Both are linked to tobacco and alcohol.

explain.caption: Relative cancer risk of the patches, lowest to highest.

options: A white patch that wipes off quite easily
A white patch that can't be rubbed off
A red patch under a denture
A blister that crusts in a week
test.why: Leukoplakia is a white patch that cannot be rubbed off and cannot be explained as any other condition. It is potentially malignant.

whyNot.0: A white patch that wipes off is thrush.
whyNot.2: A red patch under a denture is denture stomatitis.
whyNot.3: A blister that crusts is a cold sore.
